title: Elementary Concept of Superconductivity
short_intro: Superconductivity is a macroscopic quantum phenomenon characterized by the complete disappearance of electrical resistivity and the exclusion of magnetic fields below a critical temperature. It arises from the condensation of conduction electrons into bound pairs known as Cooper pairs.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic definitions of superconductivity, critical temperature T<sub>c</sub>, Meissner effect, Type-I and Type-II superconductors, and qualitative distinction from normal conductors.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: London penetration depth, London equations, Cooper pair formation mechanism via phonon-mediated interaction, isotope effect, and critical magnetic field variations.

prerequisites: Electrical resistance and resistivity in metals

concept_notes.heading: Phenomenology of Superconductivity
bullets: Superconductivity is characterized by zero electrical DC resistance when a material is cooled below its characteristic critical temperature T<sub>c</sub>.
Persistent currents can circulate in a superconducting closed loop indefinitely without any measurable decay, confirming true zero resistance.
The transition at T<sub>c</sub> is typically a thermodynamic second-order phase transition in the absence of a magnetic field, showing a discontinuity in specific heat.

concept_notes.heading: The Meissner Effect
bullets: A superconductor acts as a perfect diamagnet, expelling all magnetic flux from its interior upon transitioning to the superconducting state, a phenomenon known as the Meissner effect.
The magnetic induction B inside a bulk superconductor is identically zero (B = 0), distinct from a hypothetical perfect conductor which would merely trap existing magnetic flux.
The shielding currents flow exclusively within a very thin surface layer characterized by the London penetration depth λ.

concept_notes.heading: Type-I and Type-II Superconductors
bullets: Type-I superconductors exhibit complete Meissner effect up to a single critical magnetic field H<sub>c</sub>, above which they abruptly return to the normal state.
Type-II superconductors possess two critical fields: lower critical field H<sub>c1</sub> and upper critical field H<sub>c2</sub>, with a mixed state or vortex state existing between them.
Type-II materials maintain zero resistance up to much higher magnetic fields and temperatures, making them technically superior for high-field electromagnets.

concept_notes.heading: Microscopic Origin: BCS Theory Essentials
bullets: At the microscopic level, superconductivity is explained by the Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) theory involving the pairing of electrons mediated by lattice vibrations (phonons).
An attractive interaction between electrons via virtual phonon exchange overcomes Coulomb repulsion, forming weakly bound composite bosons called Cooper pairs.
An energy gap 2Δ opens up at the Fermi surface, requiring a finite thermal or optical energy to break the Cooper pairs and create quasi-particle excitations.

derivations.title: London Equations and Magnetic Field Penetration
derivations.conditions: Isotropic, homogeneous superconductor subjected to a static weak magnetic field
steps: Assume superconducting electrons move with velocity v<sub>s</sub> under electric field E without scattering, giving m(dv<sub>s</sub>/dt) = eE.
Express the superconducting current density as J<sub>s</sub> = n<sub>s</sub> e v<sub>s</sub>, leading to the first London equation: dJ<sub>s</sub>/dt = (n<sub>s</sub> e<sub>2</sub>/m)E.
Take the curl of the first London equation and use Maxwell's equation curl E = -(&partial;B/&partial;t) to obtain d(curl J<sub>s</sub>)/dt = -(n<sub>s</sub> e<sub>2</sub>/m)(&partial;B/&partial;t).
Integrate with respect to time and set integration constants to zero to yield the second London equation: curl J<sub>s</sub> = -(n<sub>s</sub> e<sub>2</sub>/m)B.
Combine with Ampere's law (curl B = μ<sub>0</sub> J<sub>s</sub>) to arrive at the vector Laplacian relation ∇<sup>2</sup>B = B / λ<sup>2</sup>.
derivations.result: B(x) = B(0) exp(-x / \lambda), where \lambda = \sqrt{\frac{m}{\mu_0 n_s e^2}}

derivations.title: Critical Magnetic Field Temperature Dependence
derivations.conditions: Thermodynamic derivation using free energy difference between normal and superconducting states
steps: Write the difference in Helmholtz free energy between the normal state (G<sub>n</sub>) and superconducting state (G<sub>s</sub>) in an applied magnetic field H as G<sub>n</sub>(T) - G<sub>s</sub>(T, H) = (μ<sub>0</sub> H<sub>c</sub><sup>2</sup>) / 2.
Use the Gibbs-Helmholtz thermodynamic relation and entropy differences to approximate the temperature dependence of the critical field.
Apply the empirical parabolic law observed experimentally for elemental superconductors.

formula_sheet.conditions: Valid for local superconductors at temperatures well below T_c

graphs_and_experiments.title: Resistance vs Temperature Graph (Onnes Effect)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of electrical resistance R against absolute temperature T, showing a sharp, vertical drop to absolute zero at T_c for a superconductor compared to a linear residual resistance drop for a normal metal.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the sudden loss of electrical resistivity at the critical temperature T_c.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in TGT/PGT to identify critical temperature and define the superconducting state onset.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Magnetization vs Applied Magnetic Field (Type-I vs Type-II)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Two plots: Type-I showing linear diamagnetic increase up to H_c with sudden drop to zero magnetization; Type-II showing linear diamagnetic increase up to H_c1, mixed state up to H_c2, and then zero magnetization.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Differentiates complete magnetic flux exclusion (Meissner effect) in Type-I from partial vortex penetration in Type-II superconductors.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked conceptual questions distinguishing H_c, H_c1, and H_c2.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Critical Field Curve (H_c vs T)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A parabolic curve starting at H_c(0) on the vertical axis and intersecting the horizontal temperature axis at T = T_c.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows that superconductivity is destroyed if either temperature exceeds T_c or magnetic field exceeds H_c(T).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Numerical problems involving calculation of H_c at given temperatures.

solved_numericals.question: The critical temperature of lead is 7.2 K. If the critical magnetic field at 0 K is 8.0 x 10^4 A/m, calculate the critical magnetic field at 5.0 K.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: T_c = 7.2 K, H_c(0) = 8.0 x 10^4 A/m, T = 5.0 K.
Use the empirical critical field formula: H_c(T) = H_c(0) [1 - (T/T_c)^2].

solved_numericals.question: A superconducting material has a London penetration depth of 50 nm at T = 0 K. Calculate the penetration depth at a temperature where (T/T_c)^2 = 0.19.
solution_steps: Recall the empirical Gorter-Casimir temperature dependence of penetration depth: \lambda(T) = \lambda(0) / \sqrt{1 - (T/T_c)^4}. Note: For simple estimations near low T, often approximated or used via \lambda(T) = \lambda(0) [1 - (T/T_c)^4]^{-1/2}.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the superconducting electron density n_s in a specimen given its London penetration depth \lambda = 3.5 \times 10^{-8} m, mass of electron m = 9.11 \times 10^{-31} kg, and permeability of free space \mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} H/m.
solution_steps: Start with the London penetration depth formula: \lambda = \sqrt{m / (\mu_0 n_s e^2)}.
Rearrange to solve for n_s: n_s = m / (\mu_0 e^2 \lambda^2).

assumptions_and_limitations: The London theory assumes local electrodynamics where current density is proportional to the vector potential at the exact same point.
BCS theory assumes a weak-coupling approximation and isotropic Fermi surfaces, which fails for strongly coupled or high-T_c cuprate superconductors.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A superconductor is simply a perfect conductor with zero resistance.
common_misconceptions.correct: A superconductor is a thermodynamic state characterized by zero resistance AND perfect diamagnetism (Meissner effect).
common_misconceptions.why: A perfect conductor would trap existing magnetic flux due to Lenz's law, whereas a superconductor expels all magnetic flux regardless of historical cooling path.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Superconductivity occurs only at temperatures near absolute zero.
common_misconceptions.correct: Many high-temperature superconductors (like cuprates) exhibit superconductivity at temperatures well above liquid nitrogen temperature (77 K).
common_misconceptions.why: Discovery of high-T_c superconductors shifted the operational limits far beyond liquid helium temperatures.

quick_revision: Superconductivity involves zero resistivity and complete magnetic flux expulsion (Meissner effect) below T_c.
First London Equation: \frac{\partial J_s}{\partial t} = \frac{n_s e^2}{m} E
